newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Centennial may raise AQC bid.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Centennial may raise AQC bid.

text.p: Centennial Coal Co Ltd said on Thursday it will soon decide on the wisdom of a higher bid for Allied Queensland Coalfields Ltd, thereby continuing the takeover fight with Hong Kong's Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd.
"We are still assessing the situation as to whether we will or will not increase our bid," Centennial managing director Bob Cameron told Reuters.
"But we are definitely not prepared to pay too much for the assets," he said.
Marsford Investments, a unit of CEPA, has the upper hand in the bidding with an offer of 78 cents per share which values the Brisbane-based steaming coal producer at A$21.54 million.

Centennial, which is based in Sydney and has six steaming coal mines in New South Wales and a strong Asian customer base, began the takeover battle on September 19 with an offer of 60 cents per share.
This was quickly topped by Marsford with a 70 cent per share bid, and by Centennial with its latest proposal of 75 cents.
Share market speculators have bid the stock up to a year's high of 80 cents in the hope that the fight is not yet over.

Cameron said his company would have to at least match the current Marsford offer to have a chance of winning AQC, but added that he now has other industry options which could diminish the attraction of AQC.
"We have other projects that we are seriously looking at, that we are actually negotiating on and we have done a lot of investigation into."
"So if AQC doesn't happen for us it will not be a long time before something else does."
Centennial's aim was to double annual production from the current 1.7 million tonnes in the next year or so, he said.
Cameron would not comment when asked if the production increase might be achieved by more takeover bids.
"I really can't say just at this stage," he said, noting that there was a considerable amount of Australian steaming coal acreage on the market at the moment.
The company would discuss the option of a higher bid for AQC with its trading partners before making a decision, as well as running computer models on forecast tonnages and prices.
"The issue won't remain unresolved for too much longer."
Centential believed the steaming coal outlook was better than that for coking coal in the medium to longer term.
"There are massive increases forecast in requirements for steaming coal into Asia over the next 10 years. Absolutely massive," he said.
About 30 percent of Centennial's output is used domestically and most of the remainder is sent to Asian countries.
One of its mines, Charbon, has South Korean energy group Yukong Ltd as a five percent partner.

Centennial's latest bid values AQC at A$20.71 million, a little less than half its own valuation of A$43.92 million based on Thursday's closing price of A$2.04 per share. Centennial has 21.53 million shares on issue. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
